pages.task: A timesheet: two days, each `x` hours on site plus an hour's travel, 18 hours in all. So `2(x + 1) = 18`. What is `x`?
pages.why: One day is `x + 1`, so two days are `2(x + 1) = 18`. Undo it from the right: 18 ÷ 2 = 9 hours a day, and 9 − 1 = 8. Check: `2(8 + 1) = 18`.

pages.task: Three jobs, each a £60 call-out plus `h` hours at £40 an hour, come to £420: `3(60 + 40h) = 420`. How many hours is `h`?
pages.why: One job is `60 + 40h`, so three jobs are `3(60 + 40h) = 420`. Undo it from the right: 420 ÷ 3 = £140 a job, take off the £60 call-out to leave £80, and £80 ÷ £40 = 2 hours. Check: `3(60 + 40 × 2) = 420`.

pages.task: To make `R₀` the [[subject]], the letter on its own on one side, divide both sides by the whole bracket. A warm winding reads 3.0 Ω and its bracket `1 + αΔT` is 1.2. What is `R₀`?
pages.why: `R` is `R₀` times the whole bracket, so `R₀ = R ÷ (1 + αΔT)`, and 3.0 ÷ 1.2 = 2.5 Ω. Check: `2.5 × 1.2 = 3.0`.

pages.alt: The formula R equals R nought(1 plus alpha delta T), where alpha equals 0.0039 per degrees C, and R nought equals 2.0 ohms, R equals 2.4 ohms. A flow diagram: delta T, then times alpha gives alpha delta T, then plus 1 gives 1 plus alpha delta T, then times R nought gives R. Undone from the right: 2.4, divided by R nought gives 1.2, minus 1 gives 0.2, divided by alpha gives delta T about 51. So delta T equals (R divided by R nought minus 1) divided by alpha. Put back in, 51 degrees C, so alpha delta T about 0.2 makes 2.4 against 2.4, the same. Put back in, 179 degrees C, so alpha delta T about 0.7 makes 3.4 against 2.4, not the same. The rule fits changes of about 100 °C or less, and 51 °C is inside that.

pages.text: To make `ΔT` the subject, undo the flow from the right: ÷ `R₀`, then − 1, then ÷ `α`. A winding that reads 2.0 Ω cold and 2.4 Ω after a run warmed by about 51 °C. Take the 1 off only after dividing by `R₀`, which multiplies the 1 as well: `(2.4 − 1) ÷ 2.0` gives about 179 °C.

pages.alt: The formula R equals R nought(1 plus alpha delta T), where alpha equals 0.0039 per degrees C, and R nought equals 4.0 ohms, R equals 4.6 ohms. A flow diagram: delta T, then times alpha gives alpha delta T, then plus 1 gives 1 plus alpha delta T, then times R nought gives R. Undone from the right: 4.6, divided by R nought gives 1.15, minus 1 gives 0.15, divided by alpha gives delta T about 38. Put back in, 38 degrees C, so alpha delta T about 0.15 makes 4.6 against 4.6, the same.

pages.text: The same shape turns up when metal warms. A rod or pipe warmed from `t₀` to `t₁` grows to `L₁ = L₀ + L₀α(t₁ − t₀)`, where `α` is now how much each metre grows for each degree, a different number. `L₀` is a common factor, so `L₁ = L₀(1 + α(t₁ − t₀))`, and `L₀ = L₁ ÷ (1 + α(t₁ − t₀))`, just as for `R₀`.

pages.alt: The formula L one equals L nought(1 plus alpha (t one minus t nought)), where L one equals 10.01 m, alpha (t one minus t nought) equals 0.001. A flow diagram: L nought, then times (1 plus alpha (t one minus t nought)) gives L one. Undone from the right: 10.01, divided by 1.001 gives L nought equals 10. Put back in, L nought equals 10 makes 10.01 against 10.01, the same.

pages.task: Four circuits each take `x` metres plus 2 m spare, 60 m in all: `4(x + 2) = 60`. Find `x`.
pages.why: One circuit is `x + 2`, so four are `4(x + 2) = 60`. Undo it from the right: 60 ÷ 4 = 15 m a circuit, and 15 − 2 = 13. Check: `4(13 + 2) = 60`.

pages.task: Last one. A copper coil reads 5.78 Ω after warming by 40 °C, so its bracket is 1 + 0.0039 × 40 = 1.156. What did it read cold, `R₀`?
pages.why: `R₀ = R ÷ (1 + αΔT)`, so divide by the whole bracket: 5.78 ÷ 1.156 = 5.0 Ω. Check: `5.0 × 1.156 = 5.78`.
